name: lava-flow
intent: Records what Lava Flow costs: successive well-intentioned architecture and technology changes each added on top of the last without replacing anything, so the codebase hardens into archaeological layers whose dependencies make the original design impossible to remove — and the price is that no change is reversible any more.
problem: Each generation of developers adopted a better technology, was refused a rewrite, and migrated incrementally — and the migration was never finished. The result is several complete and different ways of doing the same thing, coexisting, each with its own cost and its own fan of incoming dependencies.
context: The definition is that sub-optimal code written under development conditions is deployed to production and then expanded upon while still in a developmental state; like lava which solidifies into rock once cooled, the code becomes difficult to refactor or replace because of the dependencies that have accumulated, requiring backward compatibility with the original incomplete design. The causes named are deadline pressure turning temporary solutions into permanent ones, inadequate documentation, no automated tests making refactoring risky, and frequent team turnover losing knowledge. The AntiPatterns account is the vivid one: on a data-mining expedition through a research-originated system, developers were asked what a given class did and answered, again and again, 'I don't know what that class is for; it was written before I got here', with 30-50% of the code unowned and nobody willing to delete it for fear of breaking something nobody understood. Hadlow's Lava Layer account adds the mechanism precisely: each successive lead acted in good faith, wanted to improve the software, was refused the resources for a rewrite, and so added their own technology alongside the previous one, leaving four different ways of getting data from the database to the UI in one codebase.
benefits: It names a specific, common and underestimated failure: a rewrite is refused, an incremental migration is announced, and nobody tracks whether it completed. The failure is the incompletion, not the ambition.

The remediation is measurable and stated: resist the urge to change, understand the existing system before changing it (the Shu-ha-ri discipline applied to architecture), get management buy-in and resource allocation before starting, and use version control and change control to explore alternatives safely.

It distinguishes the two cases that look alike from the outside: the fix is not to stop improving a system but to stop starting migrations you cannot finish, and to finish or abandon the one in flight.
It explains why 'we will refactor it as we go' fails. The practitioners' objection is precise: you cannot promise to update the old code and simultaneously tell other developers not to touch it.
tradeoffs: Consistency has real value that the anti-pattern argument understates. Hadlow's conclusion is that it is sometimes better to favour consistent legacy technology over fragmentation, and that a codebase with four ways of doing the same thing is worse than one with an older but coherent approach.

Refusing every architectural change is not the alternative being proposed — a coherent older design is different from a stack of half-finished migrations. The distinction is whether one design is in charge.

Completing a migration has a real cost in a system of this size, and the honest position from the field is that the rewrite must be resourced and committed to before it starts; without buy-in and allocated capacity, it should not be started at all.
The sunk-cost objection to finishing a migration is legitimate: if the new approach is sub-optimal, replacing it again is another architectural layer.
High staff turnover is the multiplier that turns a partial migration into an archaeological record, and it is an organisational variable the technical remedy cannot control.
Some inconsistency is cheaper than its removal. Exposing messy chunks behind a facade to give them a congenial face is a legitimate first step that explicitly postpones the interior work.
quality_attributes_note: Scores describe the codebase while the smell is present. Extensibility and coupling take the worst scores, and they are worst for a specific reason rather than a general one: every newly added way of doing a thing is a new fan-in target, so the next change must consider all of them and the dependency graph has no single direction. Reliability is mid rather than low because the system runs — the damage is to the rate of safe change, not to the ability to serve traffic.

participants.responsibility: A complete approach to one problem (a data access strategy, a messaging library, a UI framework, a deployment model) added by one generation and never removed.
participants.notes: Each layer is individually defensible; the problem is that they coexist and each is now a dependency target.

participants.responsibility: The announced transition between two layers, with no completion date, no completion criteria and no owner — the mechanism by which the layers accumulate.
participants.notes: 'We'll update the old code as we touch it' is the promise that never gets followed through.

participants.responsibility: Each new lead who improved the software in good faith with whatever resources were available, and who inherited a system whose previous design decisions were not communicated.
participants.notes: Hadlow's account makes the human mechanism explicit: none of them acted in bad faith, and none had the resources to replace what they found.

use_cases: Four different data-access approaches in one application after four successive rewrites were funded partially or refused outright.
A codebase migrated 'as we go' from one ORM to another, where 40% of the code still uses the old one and the migration has been open for three years.
A monolith being converted to services, with both the in-process call path and the network call path maintained because the split is never finished.
A system carrying three generations of logging frameworks, each configured, each with its own appender and its own way of adding context.
A component library where a deprecation was announced with no removal date, so both APIs are supported indefinitely.
30-50% of a research-originated codebase being unowned, with nobody willing to delete any of it for fear of breaking something nobody understands.
avoid_when: The system is genuinely under active development and the change is small enough to complete in the current iteration — the problem is unfinished migrations, not changing technology.
The existing design is coherent and the migration's expected benefit does not justify its cost, in which case the correct decision is to stop and stay consistent.
There is no automated test coverage and no management buy-in for a funded migration, which is exactly the precondition the field guidance says must hold before starting.
You do not yet understand the existing system well enough to change it, which the Shu-ha-ri discipline treats as a prerequisite for exploration.
The inconsistency is a deliberate, temporary boundary — for example a strangler-fig migration with an explicit completion criterion, which is the opposite of lava flow because it is designed to end.
The 'application if it ain't broken, don't fix it' rule applies: it is unreasoned and sometimes right, which is the honest framing the field discussion gives it.
pitfalls: Promising an incremental migration with no completion criteria and no owner. This is the mechanism, not a symptom.
Refusing the rewrite while refusing the migration too, leaving no option and adding a layer anyway.
Believing a facade over the mess is the fix. Sweeping it under the rug gives it a congenial face and defers the work, which is legitimate as a first step and not a solution.

Removing the old layer without proving it is unused — the fear that nobody would delete dead code for fear of breaking something nobody understood is not irrational, and the cure is characterisation tests plus an owner.
Assuming the problem is the technology when it is the incompletion. Two technologies coexisting deliberately is fine; two coexisting because the second was never uninstalled is lava flow.
Letting team turnover erode the communicated design philosophy, which is the organisational precondition Hadlow identifies for the whole pattern.

related_patterns_notes.facade: A facade is the documented first step for existing lava flow: put a congenial face on the unpleasantness that has been swept under the rug, then expose it through intention-revealing selectors and hem in the growth.
related_patterns_notes.anti-corruption-layer: An anti-corruption layer is how one generation translates the previous generation's model while a migration is incomplete — the correct content for the overlap period that lava flow leaves untranslated.
related_patterns_notes.adapter: An adapter is what makes coexistence safe: each layer adapted to a stable interface means removing one is an implementation change rather than a system-wide one.
related_patterns_notes.module: A module boundary is what makes a completed migration cheap: if each approach lives in its own module behind a shared interface, the removal is a deletion.
related_patterns_notes.version-number: A deprecation with a version number and a removal date is the mechanism that distinguishes a planned migration from lava flow — one of them is designed to end.
related_patterns_notes.feature-toggle: A feature toggle can hold both implementations and route between them, which makes an incremental migration safe; the failure is that the flag outlives the migration.
related_patterns_notes.membrane: A membrane restricts the operations a domain may invoke, which bounds how far a half-migrated layer's semantics can spread.
related_patterns_notes.special-case: Special cases are how new capabilities get added beside old ones rather than through them, and they are the local mechanism by which lava flow grows.

anti_patterns: The 'we will migrate as we touch it' announcement with no completion criteria, no owner and no date, which is the mechanism that produces every layer.
Several complete ways of doing one thing coexisting, each with its own dependencies, its own configuration and its own specialists.
Announced deprecations with no removal date, so both the old and the new API are supported indefinitely and the callers never migrate.
The partially completed framework migration where a fraction of the code still uses the previous framework and nobody can say which fraction.
Unexplained code: 'I don't know what that class is for; it was written before I got here', repeated across the codebase with no path to ownership.
Architecture and technology choices recorded only in the commit history, never in a document, so each new generation re-litigates them.
Taking a new technique from a departing colleague or a conference talk and applying it to the whole codebase at once, because the demonstration was compelling.
Treating a facade over the mess as the completed refactoring rather than as the first step of one.
design_principles: Finish what you start: an architectural change is not made until the resources and the completion criteria exist, because an unfinished migration is worse than either extreme.
Consistency beats local optimality: one coherent design that is slightly older is easier to maintain than a patchwork where each part is individually newer and better.
Isolate before you replace: an adapter or a facade around the old implementation makes coexistence safe and removal cheap.
Know the system before you change it: the Shu-ha-ri discipline applied to architecture — sufficient understanding and maintenance experience before exploratory changes.
Deprecate with a date: a deprecation without a removal version is a permanent second implementation.
best_practices: Track open migrations as first-class items with an owner, a completion criterion and a date; the absence of such a list is how the layers appear.
Before starting an architectural change, ask the two questions the field asks: will the migration ever complete, and what happens if it never does? If the answer to the first is no, do not start it.
Reserve an allocation for the migration in the same plan as the new feature, because a migration funded only from leftovers never completes.
Explore alternatives in version control before adopting them — a branch, a spike, a reversible change — so exploration costs nothing and failure is acceptable.
Prefer consistency when choosing: prefer the existing technology unless the new one is measurably required by a written requirement, and say so in the decision.
Undertake one structural change at a time; overlapping architectural migrations are what produce several complete approaches rather than one.
Facade the mess first and quarantine it, then improve inward from the edge; that is the documented path and it keeps the system operable throughout.
Write the design philosophy down for the next generation — the absence of exposition is what forces every successor to re-decide.
Reduce turnover effects with pair review and by keeping build and run documentation current, so the knowledge survives the people.
sources: AntiPatterns (Bell Labs) Development AntiPattern: Lava Flow — 'hardened globules of dead code', the data-mining expedition in which developers answered 'I don't know what that class is for; it was written before I got here', 30-50% of code unowned, and the remedy: a system discovery activity to find what is actually used, delete the rest, and expect a few bugs to surface as removed dependencies.

Mike Hadlow, 'The Lava Layer Anti-Pattern' (2014), summarised in InfoQ, 'Architecture, Technology and the Lava Layer Anti-Pattern', Jan Stenberg, 2015 — the four-successive-leads account, the advice to sometimes favour consistent legacy technology, and the question of what the application looks like if the migration is never completed.

Engineering StackExchange discussion on solving lava flow — resist the urge, Shu-ha-ri before architectural change, management buy-in and resource allocation before starting, version control and change control for safe exploration, and the argument that the real problem is changes not being completed before the next one starts.
Brian Marick / AntiPatterns taxonomy cited by the Lava Flow entry.
